Enter ANTONY and DOLABELLA.

Dolabella.

1457Why would you shift it from yourself on me?
1458Can you not tell her, you must part?

Antony.

Can you not tell her, you must part? I cannot.
1459I could pull out an eye, and bid it go,
1460And t'other should not weep. O Dolabella,
1461How many deaths are in this word, Depart!
1462I dare not trust my tongue to tell her so:
1463One look of hers would thaw me into tears,
1464And I should melt, till I were lost again.

Dolabella.

1465Then let Ventidius;
1466He's rough by nature.

Antony.

1467Oh, he'll speak too harshly;
1468He'll kill her with the news: Thou, only thou.

Dolabella.

1469Nature has cast me in so soft a mould,
1470That but to hear a story, feigned for pleasure,
1471Of some sad lover's death, moistens my eyes,
1472And robs me of my manhood. I should speak
1473So faintly, with such fear to grieve her heart,
1474She'd not believe it earnest.

Antony.

She'd not believe it earnest. Therefore, –therefore
1475Thou only, thou art fit: Think thyself me;
1476And when thou speak'st (but let it first be long),
1477Take off the edge from every sharper sound,
1478And let our parting be as gently made,
1479As other loves begin: Wilt thou do this?

Dolabella.

1480What you have said so sinks into my soul,
1481That, if I must speak, I shall speak just so.

Antony.

1482I leave you then to your sad task: Farewell.
1483I sent her word to meet you.

[Goes to the door, and comes back.]

I sent her word to meet you. I forgot;
1484Let her be told, I'll make her peace with mine:
1485Her crown and dignity shall be preserved,
1486If I have power with Cæsar. –Oh, be sure
1487To think on that.

Dolabella.

To think on that. Fear not, I will remember.

[ANTONY goes again to the door, and comes back.]

Antony.

1488And tell her, too, how much I was constrained;
1489I did not this, but with extremest force:
1490Desire her not to hate my memory,
1491For I still cherish hers: –insist on that.

Dolabella.

1492Trust me, I'll not forget it.

Antony.

Trust me, I'll not forget it. Then that's all.

[Goes out, and returns again.]

1493Wilt thou forgive my fondness this once more?
1494Tell her, though we shall never meet again,
1495If I should hear she took another love,
1496The news would break my heart. – Now I must go;
1497For every time I have returned, I feel
1498My soul more tender; and my next command
1499Would be, to bid her stay, and ruin both.

[Exit.]

Dolabella.

1500Men are but children of a larger growth;
1501Our appetites as apt to change as theirs,
1502And full as craving too, and full as vain;
1503And yet the soul, shut up in her dark room,
1504Viewing so clear abroad, at home sees nothing;
1505But, like a mole in earth, busy and blind,
1506Works all her folly up, and casts it outward
1507To the world's open view: Thus I discovered,
1508And blamed the love of ruined Antony;
1509Yet wish that I were he, to be so ruined.

Enter VENTIDIUS above.

Ventidius.

1510Alone, and talking to himself? concerned too?
1511Perhaps my guess is right; he loved her once,
1512And may pursue it still.

Dolabella.

And may pursue it still. O friendship! friendship!
1513I'll canst thou answer this; and reason, worse;
1514Unfaithful in the attempt; hopeless to win;
1515And if I win, undone: mere madness all.
1516And yet the occasion's fair. What injury
1517To him, to wear the robe which he throws by!

Ventidius.

1518None, none at all. This happens as I wish,
1519To ruin her yet more with Antony.

Enter CLEOPATRA, talking with ALEXAS; CHARMION, IRAS on the other side.

Dolabella.

1520She comes! What charms have sorrow on that face!
1521Sorrow seems pleased to dwell with so much sweetness;
1522Yet, now and then, a melancholy smile
1523Breaks loose, like lightning in a winter's night,
1524And shows a moment's day.

Ventidius.

1525If she should love him too! her eunuch there?
1526That porc'pisce bodes ill weather. Draw, draw nearer,
1527Sweet devil, that I may bear.

Alexas.

Sweet devil, that I may bear. Believe me; try

[DOLABELLA goes over to CHARMION and IRAS; seems to talk with them.]

1528To make him jealous; jealousy is like
1529A polished glass held to the lips when life's in doubt;
1530If there be breath, 'twill catch the damp, and show it.

Cleopatra.

1531I grant you, jealousy's a proof of love,
1532But 'tis a weak and unavailing medicine;
1533It puts out the disease, and makes it show,
1534But has no power to cure.

Alexas.

1535'Tis your last remedy, and strongest too:
1536And then this Dolabella, who so fit
1537To practise on? He's handsome, valiant, young,
1538And looks as he were laid for nature's bait,
1539To catch weak women's eyes.
1540He stands already more than half suspected
1541Of loving you: the least kind word or glance
1542You give this youth, will kindle him with love:
1543Then, like a burning vessel set adrift,
1544You'll send him down amain before the wind,
1545To fire the heart of jealous Antony.

Cleopatra.

1546Can I do this? Ah, no; my love's so true,
1547That I can neither hide it where it is,
1548Nor show it where it is not. Nature meant me
1549A wife; a silly, harmless, household dove,
1550Fond without art, and kind without deceit;
1551But Fortune, that has made a mistress of me,
1552Has thrust me out to the wide world, unfurnished
1553Of falsehood to be happy.

Alexas.

Of falsehood to be happy. Force yourself.
1554The event will be, your lover will return,
1555Doubly desirous to possess the good
1556Which once he feared to lose.

Cleopatra.

Which once he feared to lose. I must attempt it;
1557But oh, with what regret!

[Exit ALEXAS. She comes up to DOLABELLA.]

Ventidius.

1558So, now the scene draws near; they're in my reach.

Cleopatra.

1559[to DOLABELLA.] Discoursing with my women! might not I
1560Share in your entertainment?

Charmion.

Share in your entertainment? You have been
1561The subject of it, madam.

Cleopatra.

The subject of it, madam. How! and how?

Iras.

1562Such praises of your beauty!

Cleopatra.

Such praises of your beauty! Mere poetry.
1563Your Roman wits, your Gallus and Tibullus,
1564Have taught you this from Cytheris and Delia.

Dolabella.

1565Those Roman wits have never been in Egypt;
1566Cytheris and Delia else had been unsung:
1567I, who have seen – had I been born a poet,
1568Should choose a nobler name.

Cleopatra.

Should choose a nobler name. You flatter me.
1569But, 'tis your nation's vice: All of your country
1570Are flatterers, and all false. Your friend's like you.
1571I'm sure he sent you not to speak these words.

Dolabella.

1572No, madam; yet he sent me –

Cleopatra.

No, madam; yet he sent me – Well, he sent you –

Dolabella.

1573Of a less pleasing errand.

Cleopatra.

Of a less pleasing errand. How less pleasing?
1574Less to yourself, or me?

Dolabella.

Less to yourself, or me? Madam, to both;
1575For you must mourn, and I must grieve to cause it.

Cleopatra.

1576You, Charmion, and your fellow, stand at distance. –
1577Hold up, my spirits. [Aside] Well, now your mournful matter!aparte
1578For I'm prepared, perhaps can guess it too.

Dolabella.

1579I wish you would; for 'tis a thankless office,
1580To tell ill news; And I, of all your sex,
1581Most fear displeasing you.

Cleopatra.

Most fear displeasing you. Of all your sex.
1582I soonest could forgive you, if you should.

Ventidius.

1583Most delicate advances! Woman! woman!
1584Dear, damned, inconstant sex!

Cleopatra.

Dear, damned, inconstant sex! In the first place,
1585I am to be forsaken; it's not so?

Dolabella.

1586I wish I could not answer to that question.

Cleopatra.

1587Then pass it o'er, because it troubles you:
1588I should have been more grieved another time.
1589Next, I'm to lose my kingdom –Farewell, Egypt!
1590Yes, is there any more?

Dolabella.

Yes, is there any more? Madam, I fear
1591Your too deep sense of grief has turned your reason.

Cleopatra.

1592No, no, I'm not run mad; I can bear fortune:
1593And love may be expelled by other love,
1594As poisons are by poisons.

Dolabella.

1595You o'erjoy me, madam,
1596To find your griefs so moderately borne.
1597You've heard the worst; all are not false like him.

Cleopatra.

1598No; Heaven forbid they should.

Dolabella.

1599Some men are constant.

Cleopatra.

1600And constancy deserves reward, that's certain.

Dolabella.

1601Deserves it not; but give it leave to hope.

Ventidius.

1602I'll swear, thou hast my leave. I have enough:
1603But how to manage this! Well, I'll consider.

[Exit.]

Dolabella.

1604I came prepared
1605To tell you heavy news; news, which I thought
1606Would fright the blood from your pale cheeks to hear:
1607But you have met it with a cheerfulness,
1608That makes my task more easy; and my tongue,
1609Which on another's message was employed,
1610Would gladly speak its own.

Cleopatra.

Would gladly speak its own. Hold, Dolabella.
1611First tell me, were you chosen by my lord?
1612Or sought you this employment?

Dolabella.

1613He picked me out; and, as his bosom friend,
1614He charged me with his words.

Cleopatra.

He charged me with his words. The message then
1615I know was tender, and each accent smooth,
1616To mollify that rugged word, Depart .

Dolabella.

1617Oh, you mistake: He chose the harshest words;
1618With fiery eyes, and with contracted brows,
1619He coined his face in the severest stamp;
1620And fury shook his fabric, like an earthquake;
1621He heaved for vent, and burst like bellowing Ætna,
1622In sounds scarce human – "Hence away for ever,
1623Let her begone, the blot of my renown,
1624And bane of all my hopes!"

[All the time of this speech, CLEOPATRA seems more and more concerned, till she sinks quite down.]

1625"Let her be driven, as far as men can think,
1626From man's commerce! she'll poison to the centre."

Cleopatra.

1627Oh, I can bear no more!

Dolabella.

1628Help, help! –O wretch! O cursed, cursed wretch!
1629What have I done?

Charmion.

What have I done? Help, chafe her temples, Iras.

Iras.

1630Bend, bend her forward quickly.

Charmion.

Bend, bend her forward quickly. Heaven be praised,
1631She comes again.

Cleopatra.

She comes again. Oh, let him not approach me.
1632Why have you brought me back to this loathed being,
1633The abode of falsehood, violated vows,
1634And injured love? For pity, let me go;
1635For, if there be a place of long repose,
1636I'm sure I want it. My disdainful lord
1637Can never break that quiet; nor awake
1638The sleeping soul, with hollowing in my tomb
1639Such words as fright her hence. –Unkind, unkind!

Dolabella.

1640[Kneeling.] Believe me, 'tis against myself I speak;
1641That sure desires belief; I injured him:
1642My friend ne'er spoke those words. Oh, had you seen
1643How often he came back, and every time
1644With something more obliging and more kind,
1645To add to what he said; what dear farewells;
1646How almost vanquished by his love he parted,
1647And leaned to what unwillingly he left!
1648I, traitor as I was, for love of you
1649(But what can you not do, who made me false?)
1650I forged that lie; for whose forgiveness kneels
1651This self-accused, self-punished criminal.

Cleopatra.

1652With how much ease believe we what we wish!
1653Rise, Dolabella; if you have been guilty,
1654I have contributed, and too much love
1655Has made me guilty too.
1656The advance of kindness, which I made, was feigned,
1657To call back fleeting love by jealousy;
1658But 'twould not last. Oh, rather let me lose,
1659Than so ignobly trifle with his heart.

Dolabella.

1660I find your breast fenced round from human reach,
1661Transparent as a rock of solid crystal;
1662Seen through, but never pierced. My friend, my friend,
1663What endless treasure hast thou thrown away;
1664And scattered, like an infant, in the ocean,
1665Vain sums of wealth, which none can gather thence!

Cleopatra.

1666Could you not beg
1667An hour's admittance to his private ear?
1668Like one who wanders through long barren wilds
1669And yet foreknows no hospitable inn
1670Is near to succour hunger, eats his fill,
1671Before his painful march;
1672So would I feed a while my famished eyes
1673Before we part; for I have far to go,
1674If death be far, and never must return.

VENTIDIUS, with OCTAVIA, behind.

Ventidius.

1675From hence you may discover –oh, sweet, sweet!
1676Would you indeed? The pretty hand in earnest?

Dolabella.

1677I will, for this reward.

[Takes her hand.]

I will, for this reward. Draw it not back.
1678'Tis all I e'er will beg.

Ventidius.

'Tis all I e'er will beg. They turn upon us.

Octavia.

1679What quick eyes has guilt!

Ventidius.

1680Seem not to have observed them, and go on.

They enter.

Dolabella.

1681Saw you the emperor, Ventidius?

Ventidius.

1682No.
1683I sought him; but I heard that he was private,
1684None with him but Hipparchus, his freedman.

Dolabella.

1685Know you his business?

Ventidius.

Know you his business? Giving him instructions,
1686And letters to his brother Cæsar.

Dolabella.

And letters to his brother Cæsar. Well,
1687He must be found.

[Exeunt DOLABELLA and CLEOPATRA.]

Octavia.

He must be found. Most glorious impudence!

Ventidius.

1688She looked, methought,
1689As she would say –Take your old man, Octavia;
1690Thank you, I'm better here. –
1691Well, but what use
1692Make we of this discovery?

Octavia.

Make we of this discovery? Let it die.

Ventidius.

1693I pity Dolabella; but she's dangerous;
1694Her eyes have power beyond Thessalian charms,
1695To draw the moon from heaven; for eloquence,
1696The sea-green sirens taught her voice their flattery;
1697And, while she speaks, night steals upon the day,
1698Unmarked of those that hear: Then she's so charming,
1699Age buds at sight of her, and swells to youth:
1700The holy priests gaze on her when she smiles;
1701And with heaved hands, forgetting gravity,
1702They bless her wanton eyes: Even I, who hate her,
1703With a malignant joy behold such beauty;
1704And, while I curse, desire it. Antony
1705Must needs have some remains of passion still,
1706Which may ferment into a worse relapse,
1707If now not fully cured. I know, this minute,
1708With Cæsar he's endeavouring her peace.

Octavia.

1709You have prevailed: –But for a further purpose

[Walks off.]

1710I'll prove how he will relish this discovery.
1711What, make a strumpet's peace! it swells my heart:
1712It must not, shall not be.

Ventidius.

It must not, shall not be. His guards appear.
1713Let me begin, and you shall second me.

Enter ANTONY.

Antony.

1714Octavia, I was looking you, my love:
1715What, are your letters ready? I have given
1716My last instructions.

Octavia.

My last instructions. Mine, my lord, are written.

Antony.

1717[Drawing him aside.] Ventidius.aparte

Ventidius.

[Drawing him aside.] Ventidius. My lord?

Antony.

[Drawing him aside.] Ventidius. My lord? A word in private. –aparte
1718When saw you Dolabella?

Ventidius.

When saw you Dolabella? Now, my lord,
1719He parted hence; and Cleopatra with him.

Antony.

1720Speak softly. –'Twas by my command he went,aparte
1721To bear my last farewell.

Ventidius.

To bear my last farewell. [Aloud.] It looked indeed
1722Like your farewell.

Antony.

Like your farewell. More softly. –My farewell?aparte
1723What secret meaning have you in those words
1724Of –My farewell? He did it by my order.

Ventidius.

1725[Aloud.] Then he obeyed your order. I suppose
1726You bid him do it with all gentleness,
1727All kindness, and all –love.

Antony.

All kindness, and all –love. How she mourned,aparte
1728The poor forsaken creature!

Ventidius.

1729She took it as she ought; she bore your parting
1730As she did Cæsar's, as she would another's,
1731Were a new love to come.

Antony.

Were a new love to come. [Aloud.] Thou dost belie her;
1732Most basely and maliciously belie her.

Ventidius.

1733I thought not to displease you; I have done.aparte

Octavia.

1734[Coming up.] You seemed disturbed, my lord.

Antony.

[Coming up.] You seemed disturbed, my lord. A very trifle.
1735Retire, my love.

Ventidius.

Retire, my love. It was indeed a trifle.
1736He sent –

Antony.

He sent – [Angrily.] No more. Look how thou disobey'st me;
1737Thy life shall answer it.

Octavia.

Thy life shall answer it. Then 'tis no trifle.

Ventidius.

1738[to OCTAVIA.] 'Tis less; a very nothing: You too saw it,
1739As well as I, and therefore 'tis no secret.

Antony.

1740She saw it!

Ventidius.

She saw it! Yes: She saw young Dolabella –

Antony.

1741Young Dolabella!

Ventidius.

Young Dolabella! Young, I think him young,
1742And handsome too; and so do others think him.
1743But what of that? He went by your command,
1744Indeed 'tis probable, with some kind message;
1745For she received it graciously; she smiled;
1746And then he grew familiar with her hand,
1747Squeezed it, and worried it with ravenous kisses;
1748She blushed, and sighed, and smiled, and blushed again;
1749At last she took occasion to talk softly,
1750And brought her cheek up close, and leaned on his;
1751At which, he whispered kisses back on hers;
1752And then she cried aloud –That constancy
1753Should be rewarded.

Octavia.

Should be rewarded. This I saw and heard.

Antony.

1754What woman was it, whom you heard and saw
1755So playful with my friend?
1756Not Cleopatra?

Ventidius.

1757Even she, my lord.

Antony.

Even she, my lord. My Cleopatra?

Ventidius.

1758Your Cleopatra;
1759Dolabella's Cleopatra; every man's Cleopatra.

Antony.

1760Thou liest.

Ventidius.

Thou liest. I do not lie, my lord.
1761Is this so strange? Should mistresses be left,
1762And not provide against a time of change?
1763You know she's not much used to lonely nights.

Antony.

1764I'll think no more on't.
1765I know 'tis false, and see the plot betwixt you. –
1766You needed not have gone this way, Octavia.
1767What harms it you that Cleopatra's just?
1768She's mine no more. I see, and, I forgive:
1769Urge it no further, love.

Octavia.

Urge it no further, love. Are you concerned,
1770That she's found false?

Antony.

That she's found false? I should be, were it so;
1771For, though 'tis past, I would not that the world
1772Should tax my former choice, that I loved one
1773Of so light note; but I forgive you both.

Ventidius.

1774What has my age deserved, that you should think
1775I would abuse your ears with perjury?
1776If Heaven be true, she's false.

Antony.

1777Though heaven and earth
1778Should witness it, I'll not believe her tainted.

Ventidius.

1779I'll bring you, then, a witness
1780From hell, to prove her so. –Nay, go not back;

[Seeing ALEXAS just entering, and starting back.]

1781For stay you must and shall.

Alexas.

For stay you must and shall. What means my lord?

Ventidius.

1782To make you do what most you hate, –speak truth.
1783You are of Cleopatra's private counsel,
1784Of her bed-counsel, her lascivious hours;
1785Are conscious of each nightly change she makes,
1786And watch her, as Chaldeans do the moon,
1787Can tell what signs she passes through, what day.

Alexas.

1788My noble lord!

Ventidius.

My noble lord! My most illustrious pander,
1789No fine set speech, no cadence, no turned periods,
1790But a plain homespun truth, is what I ask:
1791I did, myself, o'erhear your queen make love
1792To Dolabella. Speak; for I will know,
1793By your confession, what more passed betwixt them;
1794How near the business draws to your employment;
1795And when the happy hour.

Antony.

1796Speak truth, Alexas; whether it offend
1797Or please Ventidius, care not: Justify
1798Thy injured queen from malice: Dare his worst.

Octavia.

1799[aside] See how he gives him courage! how he fearsaparte
1800To find her false! and shuts his eyes to truth,
1801Willing to be misled!

Alexas.

1802As far as love may plead for woman's frailty,
1803Urged by desert and greatness of the lover,
1804So far, divine Octavia, may my queen
1805Stand even excused to you for loving him
1806Who is your lord: so far, from brave Ventidius,

Antony.

1808'Tis well, and truly spoken: mark, Ventidius.

Alexas.

1809To you, most noble emperor, her strong passion
1810Stands not excused, but wholly justified.
1811Her beauty's charms alone, without her crown,
1812From Ind and Meroe drew the distant vows
1813Of sighing kings; and at her feet were laid

1816She thought a Roman only could deserve her,
1817And, of all Romans, only Antony;
1818And, to be less than wife to you, disdained
1819Their lawful passion.

Antony.

Their lawful passion. 'Tis but truth.

Alexas.

1820And yet, though love, and your unmatched desert,
1821Have drawn her from the due regard of honour,
1822At last Heaven opened her unwilling eyes
1823To see the wrongs she offered fair Octavia,
1824Whose holy bed she lawlessly usurped.
1825The sad effects of this improsperous war
1826Confirmed those pious thoughts.

Ventidius.

Confirmed those pious thoughts. [aside] Oh, wheel you there?aparte
1827Observe him now; the man begins to mend,
1828And talk substantial reason. –Fear not, eunuch;
1829The emperor has given thee leave to speak.

Alexas.

1830Else had I never dared to offend his ears
1831With what the last necessity has urged
1832On my forsaken mistress; yet I must not
1833Presume to say, her heart is wholly altered.

Antony.

1834No, dare not for thy life, I charge thee dare not
1835Pronounce that fatal word!

Octavia.

1836[Aside.] Must I bear this? Good Heaven, afford me patience.aparte

Ventidius.

1837On, sweet eunuch; my dear half-man, proceed.

Alexas.

1838Yet Dolabella
1839Has loved her long; he, next my god-like lord,
1840Deserves her best; and should she meet his passion,
1841Rejected, as she is, by him she loved –

Antony.

1842Hence from my sight! for I can bear no more:
1843Let furies drag thee quick to hell; let all
1844The longer damned have rest; each torturing hand
1845Do thou employ, till Cleopatra comes;
1846Then join thou too, and help to torture her!

Octavia.

1847'Tis not well,
1848Indeed, my lord, 'tis much unkind to me,
1849To show this passion, this extreme concernment,
1850For an abandoned, faithless prostitute.

Antony.

1851Octavia, leave me; I am much disordered:
1852Leave me, I say.

Octavia.

Leave me, I say. My lord!

Antony.

Leave me, I say. My lord! I bid you leave me.

Ventidius.

1853Obey him, madam: best withdraw a while,
1854And see how this will work.

Octavia.

1855Wherein have I offended you, my lord,
1856That I am bid to leave you? Am I false,
1857Or infamous? Am I a Cleopatra?
1858Were I she,
1859Base as she is, you would not bid me leave you;
1860But hang upon my neck, take slight excuses,
1861And fawn upon my falsehood.

Antony.

And fawn upon my falsehood. 'Tis too much.
1862Too much, Octavia; I am pressed with sorrows
1863Too heavy to be borne: and you add more:
1864I would retire, and recollect what's left
1865Of man within, to aid me.

Octavia.

Of man within, to aid me. You would mourn,
1866In private, for your love, who has betrayed you.
1867You did but half return to me: your kindness
1868Lingered behind with her. I hear, my lord,
1869You make conditions for her,
1870And would include her treaty. Wondrous proofs
1871Of love to me!

Antony.

Of love to me! Are you my friend, Ventidius?
1872Or are you turned a Dolabella too,
1873And let this fury loose?

Ventidius.

And let this fury loose? Oh, be advised,
1874Sweet madam, and retire.

Octavia.

1875Yes, I will go; but never to return.
1876You shall no more be haunted with this Fury.
1877My lord, my lord, love will not always last,
1878When urged with long unkindness and disdain:
1879Take her again, whom you prefer to me;
1880She stays but to be called. Poor cozened man!
1881Let a feigned parting give her back your heart,
1882Which a feigned love first got; for injured me,
1883Though my just sense of wrongs forbid my stay,
1884My duty shall be yours.
1885To the dear pledges of our former love
1886My tenderness and care shall be transferred,
1887And they shall cheer, by turns, my widowed nights:
1888So, take my last farewell; for I despair
1889To have you whole, and scorn to take you half.

[Exit.]

Ventidius.

1890I combat Heaven, which blasts my best designs:
1891My last attempt must be to win her back;
1892But oh! I fear in vain.

[Exit.]

Antony.

1893Why was I framed with this plain, honest heart,
1894Which knows not to disguise its griefs and weakness,
1895But bears its working outward to the world?
1896I should have kept the mighty anguish in,
1897And forced a smile at Cleopatra's falsehood:
1898Octavia had believed it, and had stayed.
1899But I am made a shallow-forded stream,
1900Seen to the bottom: all my clearness scorned,
1901And all my faults exposed. –See where he comes,

Enter DOLABELLA.

1902Who has profaned the sacred name of friend,
1903And worn it into vileness!
1904With how secure a brow, and specious form
1905He gilds the secret villain! Sure that face
1906Was meant for honesty; but Heaven mismatched it,
1907And furnished treason out with nature's pomp,
1908To make its work more easy.

Dolabella.

To make its work more easy. O my friend!

Antony.

1909Well, Dolabella, you performed my message?

Dolabella.

1910I did, unwillingly.

Antony.

I did, unwillingly. Unwillingly?
1911Was it so hard for you to bear our parting?
1912You should have wished it.

Dolabella.

You should have wished it. Why?

Antony.

You should have wished it. Why? Because you love me.
1913And she received my message with as true,
1914With as unfeigned a sorrow as you brought it?

Dolabella.

1915She loves you, even to madness.

Antony.

She loves you, even to madness. Oh, I know it.
1916You, Dolabella, do not better know
1917How much she loves me. And should I
1918Forsake this beauty? This all-perfect creature?

Dolabella.

1919I could not, were she mine.

Antony.

I could not, were she mine. And yet you first
1920Persuaded me: How come you altered since?

Dolabella.

1921I said at first I was not fit to go:
1922I could not hear her sighs, and see her tears,
1923But pity must prevail: And so, perhaps,
1924It may again with you; for I have promised,
1925That she should take her last farewell: And, see,
1926She comes to claim my word.

Enter CLEOPATRA.

Antony.

She comes to claim my word. False Dolabella!

Dolabella.

1927What's false, my lord?

Antony.

What's false, my lord? Why, Dolabella's false,
1928And Cleopatra's false; both false and faithless.
1929Draw near, you well-joined wickedness, you serpents,
1930Whom I have in my kindly bosom warmed,
1931Till I am stung to death.

Dolabella.

Till I am stung to death. My lord, have I
1932Deserved to be thus used?

Cleopatra.

Deserved to be thus used? Can Heaven prepare
1933A newer torment? Can it find a curse
1934Beyond our separation?

Antony.

Beyond our separation? Yes, if fate
1935Be just, much greater: Heaven should be ingenious
1936In punishing such crimes. The rolling stone
1937And gnawing vulture were slight pains, invented
1938When Jove was young, and no examples known
1939Of mighty ills; but you have ripened sin,
1940To such a monstrous growth, 'twill pose the gods
1941To find an equal torture. Two, two such! –
1942Oh, there's no further name, –two such! to me,
1943To me, who locked my soul within your breasts,
1944Had no desires, no joys, no life, but you;
1945When half the globe was mine, I gave it you
1946In dowry with my heart; I had no use,
1947No fruit of all, but you; A friend and mistress
1948Was what the world could give. O Cleopatra!
1949O Dolabella! how could you betray
1950This tender heart, which with an infant fondness
1951Lay lulled betwixt your bosoms, and there slept,
1952Secure of injured faith?

Dolabella.

1953If she has wronged you,
1954Heaven, hell, and you revenge it.

Antony.

1955If she has wronged me!
1956Thou wouldst evade thy part of guilt; but swear
1957Thou lov'st not her.

Dolabella.

Thou lov'st not her. Not so as I love you.

Antony.

1958Not so? Swear, swear, I say, thou dost not love her.

Dolabella.

1959No more than friendship will allow.

Antony.

No more than friendship will allow. No more?
1960Friendship allows thee nothing: Thou art perjured –
1961And yet thou didst not swear thou lov'st her not;
1962But not so much, no more. O trifling hypocrite,
1963Who dar'st not own to her, thou dost not love,
1964Nor own to me, thou dost! Ventidius heard it;
1965Octavia saw it.

Cleopatra.

Octavia saw it. They are enemies.

Antony.

1966Alexas is not so: He, he confessed it;
1967He, who, next hell, best knew it, he avowed it.

[To DOLABELLA.]

1968Why do I seek a proof beyond yourself?
1969You, whom I sent to bear my last farewell,
1970Returned, to plead her stay.

Dolabella.

Returned, to plead her stay. What shall I answer?
1971If to have loved be guilt, then I have sinned;
1972But if to have repented of that love
1973Can wash away my crime, I have repented.
1974Yet, if I have offended past forgiveness,
1975Let not her suffer: She is innocent.

Cleopatra.

1976Ah, what will not a woman do, who loves?
1977What means will she refuse, to keep that heart,
1978Where all her joys are placed? 'Twas I encouraged,
1979'Twas I blew up the fire that scorched his soul,
1980To make you jealous, and by that regain you.
1981But all in vain; I could not counterfeit:
1982In spite of all the dams my love broke o'er,
1983And drowned my heart again: fate took the occasion;
1984And thus one minute's feigning has destroyed
1985My whole life's truth.

Antony.

My whole life's truth. Thin cobweb arts of falsehood;
1986Seen, and broke through at first.

Dolabella.

Seen, and broke through at first. Forgive your mistress.

Cleopatra.

1987Forgive your friend.

Antony.

Forgive your friend. You have convinced yourselves.
1988You plead each other's cause: What witness have you,
1989That you but meant to raise my jealousy?

Cleopatra.

1990Ourselves, and Heaven.

Antony.

1991Guilt witnesses for guilt. Hence, love and friendship!
1992You have no longer place in human breasts,
1993These two have driven you out: Avoid my sight!
1994I would not kill the man whom I have loved,
1995And cannot hurt the woman; but avoid me:
1996I do not know how long I can be tame;
1997For, if I stay one minute more, to think
1998How I am wronged, my justice and revenge
1999Will cry so loud within me, that my pity
2000Will not be heard for either.

Dolabella.

Will not be heard for either. Heaven has but
2001Our sorrow for our sins; and then delights
2002To pardon erring man: Sweet mercy seems
2003Its darling attribute, which limits justice;
2004As if there were degrees in infinite,
2005And infinite would rather want perfection
2006Than punish to extent.

Antony.

Than punish to extent. I can forgive
2007A foe; but not a mistress and a friend.
2008Treason is there in its most horrid shape,
2009Where trust is greatest; and the soul resigned,
2010Is stabbed by its own guards: I'll hear no more;
2011Hence from my sight for ever!

Cleopatra.

Hence from my sight for ever! How? for ever!
2012I cannot go one moment from your sight,
2013And must I go for ever?
2014My joys, my only joys, are centred here:
2015What place have I to go to? My own kingdom?
2016That I have lost for you: Or to the Romans?
2017They hate me for your sake: Or must I wander
2018The wide world o'er, a helpless, banished woman,
2019Banished for love of you; banished from you?
2020Ay, there's the banishment! Oh, hear me; hear me,
2021With strictest justice: For I beg no favour;
2022And if I have offended you, then kill me,
2023But do not banish me.

Antony.

But do not banish me. I must not hear you.
2024I have a fool within me takes your part;
2025But honour stops my ears.

Cleopatra.

But honour stops my ears. For pity hear me!
2026Would you cast off a slave who followed you?
2027Who crouched beneath your spurn? –He has no pity!
2028See, if he gives one tear to my departure;
2029One look, one kind farewell: O iron heart!
2030Let all the gods look down, and judge betwixt us,
2031If he did ever love!

Antony.

If he did ever love! No more: Alexas!

Dolabella.

2032A perjured villain!

Antony.

A perjured villain! [to Cleopatra.] Your Alexas; yours.

Cleopatra.

2033Oh, 'twas his plot; his ruinous design,
2034To engage you in my love by jealousy.
2035Hear him; confront him with me; let him speak.

Antony.

2036I have; I have.

Cleopatra.

I have; I have. And if he clear me not –

Antony.

2037Your creature! one who hangs upon your smiles!
2038Watches your eye, to say or to unsay,
2039Whate'er you please! I am not to be moved.

Cleopatra.

2040Then must we part? Farewell, my cruel lord!
2041The appearance is against me; and I go,
2042Unjustified, for ever from your sight.
2043How I have loved, you know; how yet I love,
2044My only comfort is, I know myself:
2045I love you more, even now you are unkind,
2046Than when you loved me most; so well, so truly
2047I'll never strive against it; but die pleased,

Antony.

2049Good heaven, they weep at parting!
2050Must I weep too? that calls them innocent.
2051I must not weep; and yet I must, to think
2052That I must not forgive. –
2053Live, but live wretched; 'tis but just you should,
2054Who made me so: Live from each other's sight:
2055Let me not hear you meet. Set all the earth,
2056And all the seas, betwixt your sundered loves:
2057View nothing common but the sun and skies.
2058Now, all take several ways;
2059And each your own sad fate, with mine, deplore;
2060That you were false, and I could trust no more.

[Exeunt severally.]

ACT V

SCENE I

Enter CLEOPATRA, CHARMION, and IRAS.

Charmion.

2061Be juster, Heaven; such virtue punished thus,
2062Will make us think that chance rules all above,
2063And shuffles, with a random hand, the lots
2064Which man is forced to draw.

Cleopatra.

2065I could tear out these eyes that gained his heart,
2066And had not power to keep it. O the curse
2067Of doting on, even when I find it dotage!
2068Bear witness, gods, you heard him bid me go;
2069You, whom he mocked with imprecating vows

2071You may hold me –

[She pulls out her dagger, and they hold her.]

2072But I can keep my breath; I can die inward,
2073And choke this love.

Enter ALEXAS.

Iras.

And choke this love. Help, O Alexas, help!
2074The queen grows desperate; her soul struggles in her
2075With all the agonies of love and rage,
2076And strives to force its passage.

Cleopatra.

And strives to force its passage. Let me go.
2077Art thou there, traitor! –O,
2078O for a little breath, to vent my rage,
2079Give, give me away, and let me loose upon him.

Alexas.

2080Yes, I deserve it, for my ill-timed truth.
2081Was it for me to prop
2082The ruins of a falling majesty?
2083To place myself beneath the mighty flaw,
2084Thus to be crushed, and pounded into atoms,
2085By its o'erwhelming weight? 'Tis too presuming
2086For subjects to preserve that wilful power,
2087Which courts its own destruction.

Cleopatra.

Which courts its own destruction. I would reason
2088More calmly with you. Did not you o'errule,
2089And force my plain, direct, and open love,
2090Into these crooked paths of jealousy?
2091Now, what's the event? Octavia is removed;
2092But Cleopatra's banished. Thou, thou villain,
2093Hast pushed my boat to open sea; to prove,
2094At my sad cost, if thou canst steer it back.
2095It cannot be; I'm lost too far; I'm ruined:
2096Hence, thou impostor, traitor, monster, devil! –
2097I can no more: Thou, and my griefs, have sunk
2098Me down so low, that I want voice to curse thee.

Alexas.

2099Suppose some shipwrecked seaman near the shore,
2100Dropping and faint with climbing up the cliff,
2101If, from above, some charitable hand
2102Pull him to safety, hazarding himself,
2103To draw the other's weight; would he look back,
2104And curse him for his pains? The case is yours;
2105But one step more, and you have gained the height.

2106Sunk, never more to rise.

Alexas.

2107Octavia's gone, and Dolabella banished.
2108Believe me, madam, Antony is yours.
2109His heart was never lost, but started off
2110To jealousy, love's last retreat and covert;
2111Where it lies hid in shades, watchful in silence,
2112And listening for the sound that calls it back.
2113Some other, any man ('tis so advanced),
2114May perfect this unfinished work, which I
2115(Unhappy only to myself) have left
2116So easy to his hand.

Cleopatra.

So easy to his hand. Look well thou do't; else –

Alexas.

2117Else, what your silence threatens. – Antony
2118Is mounted up the Pharos; from whose turret,
2119He stands surveying our Egyptian galleys,
2120Engaged with Cæsar's fleet. Now death or conquest!
2121If the first happen, fate acquits my promise;
2122If we o'ercome, the conqueror is yours.

[A distant shout within.]

Charmion.

2123Have comfort, madam: Did you mark that shout?

[Second shout nearer.]

2124Hark! they redouble it.

Alexas.

Hark! they redouble it. 'Tis from the port.
2125The loudness shows it near: Good news, kind heavens!

Cleopatra.

2126Osiris make it so!

Serapion.

Osiris make it so! Where, where's the queen?

Alexas.

2127How frightfully the holy coward stares
2128As if not yet recovered of the assault,
2129When all his gods, and, what's more dear to him,
2130His offerings, were at stake.

Serapion.

His offerings, were at stake. O horror, horror!
2131Egypt has been; our latest hour has come:
2132The queen of nations, from her ancient seat,
2133Is sunk for ever in the dark abyss:
2134Time has unrolled her glories to the last,
2135And now closed up the volume.

Cleopatra.

2136Say, whence thou comest; though fate is in thy face,

And threatens ere thou speakest. I came from Pharos;
2139From viewing (spare me, and imagine it)
2140Our land's last hope, your navy –

2141They fought not.

2142With Antony, your well-appointed fleet

Serapion.

2160His fury cannot be expressed by words:
2161Thrice he attempted headlong to have fallen
2162Full on his foes, and aimed at Cæsar's galley:

2164Should he now find you –

Alexas.

Should he now find you – Shun him; seek your safety,
2165Till you can clear your innocence.

Alexas.

2166You must not; haste you to your monument,
2167While I make speed to Cæsar.

Cleopatra.

While I make speed to Cæsar. Cæsar! No,
2168I have no business with him.

I have no business with him. I can work him

Cleopatra.

2170Base fawning wretch! wouldst thou betray him too?
2171Hence from my sight! I will not hear a traitor;

2173Serapion, thou art honest; counsel me:

Serapion.

2175Retire; you must not yet see Antony.
2176He who began this mischief,
2177'Tis just he tempt the danger; let him clear you:
2178And, since he offered you his servile tongue,

Alexas.

2187O pity me, and let me follow you.

2188To death, if thou stir hence. Speak, if thou canst,

Alexas.

2191O that I less could fear to lose this being,
2192Which, like a snowball in my coward hand,
2193The more 'tis grasped, the faster melts away.
2194Poor reason! what a wretched aid art thou!
2195For still, in spite of thee,
2196These two long lovers, soul and body, dread

2199No matter what becomes of Cleopatra.

Antony.

2200[Within.] Which way? where?

Ventidius.

Alexas.

2201Ah me! I hear him; yet I'm unprepared:
2202My gift of lying's gone;
2203And this court-devil, which I so oft have raised,

Enter ANTONY and VENTIDIUS.

Antony.

2206O happy Cæsar! thou hast men to lead:
2207Think not 'tis thou hast conquered Antony;
2208But Rome has conquered Egypt. I'm betrayed.

Ventidius.

2209Curse on this treacherous train!
2210Their soil and heaven infect them all with baseness:
2211And their young souls come tainted to the world
2212With the first breath they draw.

Antony.

2213The original villain sure no god created;
2214He was a bastard of the sun, by Nile,
2215Aped into man; with all his mother's mud
2216Crusted about his soul.

Ventidius.

Crusted about his soul. The nation is
2217One universal traitor; and their queen
2218The very spirit and extract of them all.

Antony.

2219Is there yet left
2220A possibility of aid from valour?
2221Is there one god unsworn to my destruction?
2222The least unmortgaged hope? for, if there be,
2223Methinks I cannot fall beneath the fate
2224Of such a boy as Cæsar.
2225The world's one half is yet in Antony;
2226And from each limb of it that's hewed away,
2227The soul comes back to me.

Ventidius.

The soul comes back to me. There yet remain
2228Three legions in the town. The last assault
2229Lopt off the rest; if death be your design, –
2230As I must wish it now, –these are sufficient
2231To make a heap about us of dead foes,
2232An honest pile for burial.

Antony.

An honest pile for burial. They are enough.
2233We'll not divide our stars; but, side by side,
2234Fight emulous, and with malicious eyes
2235Survey each other's acts: So every death
2236Thou giv'st, I'll take on me, as a just debt,
2237And pay thee back a soul.

Ventidius.

2238Now you shall see I love you. Not a word
2239Of chiding more. By my few hours of life,
2240I am so pleased with this brave Roman fate,
2241That I would not be Cæsar, to outlive you.
2242When we put off this flesh, and mount together,
2243I shall be shown to all the ethereal crowd, –
2244Lo, this is he who died with Antony!

Antony.

2245Who knows, but we may pierce through all their troops,
2246And reach my veterans yet? 'tis worth the 'tempting,
2247To o'erleap this gulf of fate,
2248And leave our wond'ring destinies behind.

Enter ALEXAS, trembling.

Ventidius.

2249See, see, that villain!
2250See Cleopatra stamped upon that face,
2251With all her cunning, all her arts of falsehood!
2252How she looks out through those dissembling eyes!
2253How he has set his countenance for deceit,
2254And promises a lie, before he speaks!
2255Let me despatch him first.

[Drawing.]

Alexas.

Let me despatch him first. O spare me, spare me!

Antony.

2256Hold; he's not worth your killing. –On thy life,
2257Which thou may'st keep, because I scorn to take it,
2258No syllable to justify thy queen;
2259Save thy base tongue its office.

Alexas.

Save thy base tongue its office. Sir, she is gone,
2260Where she shall never be molested more
2261By love, or you.

Antony.

By love, or you. Fled to her Dolabella!
2262Die, traitor! I revoke my promise! die!

[Going to kill him.]

Alexas.

2263O hold! she is not fled.

Antony.

O hold! she is not fled. She is: my eyes
2264Are open to her falsehood; my whole life
2265Has been a golden dream of love and friendship;
2266But, now I wake, I'm like a merchant, roused
2267From soft repose, to see his vessel sinking,
2268And all his wealth cast over. Ungrateful woman!
2269Who followed me, but as the swallow summer,
2270Hatching her young ones in my kindly beams,
2271Singing her flatteries to my morning wake:
2272But, now my winter comes, she spreads her wings,
2273And seeks the spring of Cæsar.

Alexas.

And seeks the spring of Cæsar. Think not so:
2274Her fortunes have, in all things, mixed with yours.
2275Had she betrayed her naval force to Rome,
2276How easily might she have gone to Cæsar,
2277Secure by such a bribe!

Ventidius.

Secure by such a bribe! She sent it first,
2278To be more welcome after.

Antony.

To be more welcome after. 'Tis too plain;
2279Else would she have appeared, to clear herself.

Alexas.

2280Too fatally she has: she could not bear
2281To be accused by you; but shut herself
2282Within her monument; looked down and sighed;
2283While, from her unchanged face, the silent tears
2284Dropt, as they had not leave, but stole their parting.
2285Some undistinguished words she inly murmured;
2286Al last, she raised her eyes; and, with such looks
2287As dying Lucrece cast –

Antony.

As dying Lucrece cast – My heart forebodes –

Ventidius.

2288All for the best: –Go on.

Alexas.

All for the best: –Go on. She snatched her poniard,
2289And, ere we could prevent the fatal blow,
2290Plunged it within her breast; then turned to me:
2291Go, bear my lord, said she, my last farewell;
2292And ask him, if he yet suspect my faith.
2293More she was saying, but death rushed betwixt.
2294She half pronounced your name with her last breath,
2295And buried half within her.

Ventidius.

And buried half within her. Heaven be praised!

Antony.

2296Then art thou innocent, my poor dear love,
2297And art thou dead?
2298O those two words! their sound should be divided:
2299Hadst thou been false, and died; or hadst thou lived,
2300And hadst been true –But innocence and death!
2301This shows not well above. Then what am I,
2302The murderer of this truth, this innocence!
2303Thoughts cannot form themselves in words so horrid
2304As can express my guilt!

Ventidius.

2305Is't come to this? The gods have been too gracious;
2306And thus you thank them for it!

Antony.

2307[to ALEXAS.] Why stayest thou here?
2308Is it for thee to spy upon my soul,
2309And see its inward mourning? Get thee hence;
2310Thou art not worthy to behold, what now
2311Becomes a Roman emperor to perform.

Alexas.

2312He loves her still:
2313His grief betrays it. Good! the joy to find
2314She's yet alive, completes the reconcilement.

2316Fate comes too fast upon my wit,
2317Hunts me too hard, and meets me at each double.

Ventidius.

2318[Aside.] Would she had died a little sooner, though!aparte
2319Before Octavia went, you might have treated:
2320Now 'twill look tame, and would not be received.
2321Come, rouse yourself, and let's die warm together.

Antony.

2322I will not fight: there's no more work for war.
2323The business of my angry hours is done.

Ventidius.

2324Cæsar is at your gates.

Antony.

Cæsar is at your gates. Why, let him enter;
2325He's welcome now.

Ventidius.

He's welcome now. What lethargy has crept into your soul?

Antony.

2326'Tis but a scorn of life, and just desire

Ventidius.

2328Do it bravely.

Antony.

2329I will; but not by fighting. O Ventidius!
2330What should I fight for now? –my queen is dead.
2331I was but great for her; my power, my empire,
2332Were but my merchandise to buy her love;
2333And conquered kings, my factors. Now she's dead,
2334Let Cæsar take the world, –
2335An empty circle, since the jewel's gone

Ventidius.

2338Would you be taken?

Antony.

Would you be taken? Yes, I would be taken;
2339But, as a Roman ought, –dead, my Ventidius:
2340For I'll convey my soul from Cæsar's reach,
2341And lay down life myself. 'Tis time the world
2342Should have a lord, and know whom to obey.
2343We two have kept its homage in suspense,
2344And bent the globe, on whose each side we trod,
2345Till it was dented inwards. Let him walk
2346Alone upon't: I'm weary of my part.
2347My torch is out; and the world stands before me,
2348Like a black desert at the approach of night:
2349I'll lay me down, and stray no farther on.

Ventidius.

2350I could be grieved,
2351But that I'll not outlive you: choose your death;
2352For, I have seen him in such various shapes,
2353I care not which I take: I'm only troubled,
2354The life I bear is worn to such a rag,
2355'Tis scarce worth giving. I could wish, indeed,
2356We threw it from us with a better grace;

2358We might at least thrust out our paws, and wound

Antony.

2360I have thought on it.
2361Ventidius, you must live.

Ventidius.

Ventidius, you must live. I must not, sir.

Antony.

2362Wilt thou not live, to speak some good of me?
2363To stand by my fair fame, and guard the approaches

Ventidius.

From the ill tongues of men? Who shall guard mine,
2365For living after you?

Antony.

For living after you? Say, I command it.

Ventidius.

2366If we die well, our deaths will speak themselves

Antony.

And need no living witness. Thou hast loved me,
2368And fain I would reward thee. I must die;
2369Kill me, and take the merit of my death,
2370To make thee friends with Cæsar.

Ventidius.

To make thee friends with Cæsar. Thank your kindness.
2371You said I loved you; and in recompense,

With a hard thought of you? Forgive me, Roman.
2375Since I have heard of Cleopatra's death,
2376My reason bears no rule upon my tongue,

2379By Heaven I will not.

Antony.

2381Kill me first,

Ventidius.

Thy friend before thyself. Give me your hand.
2384We soon shall meet again. Now, farewell, emperor! –

[Embrace.]

2385Methinks that word's too cold to be my last:
2386Since death sweeps all distinctions, farewell, friend!
2387That's all –
2388I will not make a business of a trifle;

Antony.

Pray turn your face. I do: strike home, be sure.

Ventidius.

2391Home as my sword will reach.

[Kills himself.]

Home as my sword will reach. Oh, thou mistak'st;

2397Rather than kill my friend.

Antony.

2398Farewell! Ever my leader, even in death!
2399My queen and thou have got the start of me,
2400And I'm the lag of honour . –Gone so soon?
2401Is Death no more? he used him carelessly,
2402With a familiar kindness: ere he knocked,
2403Ran to the door, and took him in his arms,
2404As who should say –You're welcome at all hours,
2405A friend need give no warning. Books had spoiled him;
2406For all the learned are cowards by profession.
2407'Tis not worth
2408My further thought; for death, for aught I know,
2409Is but to think no more. Here's to be satisfied.

2410I've missed my heart. O unperforming hand!
2411Thou never couldst have erred in a worse time.
2412My fortune jades me to the last; and death,
2413Like a great man, takes state, and makes me wait

[Trampling within.]

2415Some, perhaps, from Cæsar:
2416If he should find me living, and suspect
2417That I played booty with my life! I'll mend

[Rises upon his knees.]

Cleopatra.

2419Where is my lord? where is he?

Charmion.

Where is my lord? where is he? There he lies,
2420And dead Ventidius by him.

Cleopatra.

2421My fears were prophets; I am come too late.

Antony.

2423Or am I dead before I knew, and thou
2424The first kind ghost that meets me?

The first kind ghost that meets me? Help me seat him.
2425Send quickly, send for help!

[They place him in a chair.]

Antony.

Send quickly, send for help! I am answered.
2426We live both. Sit thee down, my Cleopatra:
2427I'll make the most I can of life, to stay
2428A moment more with thee.

Cleopatra.

A moment more with thee. How is it with you?

Antony.

2429'Tis as with a man
2430Removing in a hurry; all packed up,
2431But one dear jewel that his haste forgot;
2432And he, for that, returns upon the spur:
2433So I come back for thee.

Cleopatra.

2434Too long, ye heavens, you have been cruel to me:

2437I keep my soul by force.

Say but, thou art not false. 'Tis now too late

2442This fatal consequence. My fleet betrayed

Antony.

Both you and me. And Dolabella –

Cleopatra.

Both you and me. And Dolabella – Scarce
2444Esteemed before he loved; but hated now.

Antony.

2445Enough: my life's not long enough for more.
2446Thou say'st, thou wilt come after: I believe thee;
2447For I can now believe whate'er thou sayest,
2448That we may part more kindly.

Cleopatra.

That we may part more kindly. I will come:
2449Doubt not, my life, I'll come, and quickly too:
2450Cæsar shall triumph o'er no part of thee.

Antony.

2451But grieve not, while thou stayest,
2452My last disastrous times:
2453Think we have had a clear and glorious day
2454And Heaven did kindly to delay the storm,
2455Just till our close of evening. Ten years' love,
2456And not a moment lost, but all improved
2457To the utmost joys, –what ages have we lived?

2459While hand in hand we walk in groves below,

2462Your words are like the notes of dying swans,
2463Too sweet to last. Were there so many hours

Antony.

2465No, not a minute. –This one kiss –more worth

Cleopatra.

2467O tell me so again,
2468And take ten thousand kisses for that word.
2469My lord, my lord! speak, if you yet have being;
2470Sign to me, if you cannot speak; or cast

2472He's gone too far to hear you;
2473And this you see, a lump of senseless clay,

The leavings of a soul. Remember, madam,

He charged you not to grieve. And I'll obey him.
2476I have not loved a Roman, not to know

2479And now I'll not die less. Let dull Octavia

For Roman laws to break. Will you then die?

Cleopatra.

2483Why shouldst thou make that question?

Why shouldst thou make that question? Cæsar is merciful.

Cleopatra.

2484Let him be so

2486Made no such covenant with him, to spare me

I'll none of that. Whatever you resolve,

I'll follow, even to death. I only feared

Cleopatra.

2496Why, now, 'tis as it should be, Quick, my friends,

2499Lest I should be surprising;
2500Keep him not waiting for his love too long.
2501You, Charmion, bring my crown and richest jewels;

2505The aspics, madam?

2506'Tis sweet to die, when they would force life on me,
2507To rush into the dark abode of death,
2508And seize him first; if he be like my love,
2509He is not frightful, sure.
2510We're now alone, in secrecy and silence;
2511And is not this like lovers? I may kiss
2512These pale, cold lips; Octavia does not see me:
2513And, oh! 'tis better far to have him thus,

Charmion.

2515What must be done?

What must be done? Short ceremony, friends;
2516But yet it must be decent. First, this laurel

Wert worthy so to triumph. To what end

2522Dull, that thou art! why 'tis to meet my love;

And dress the bride of Antony. 'Tis done.

Cleopatra.

2528Now seat me by my lord. I claim this place;

Reach me the casket. Underneath the fruit

Cleopatra.

The aspic lies. Welcome, thou kind deceiver!

[Putting aside the leaves.]

2537Thou best of thieves; who, with an easy key,
2538Dost open life, and, unperceived by us,

And thinks himself but sleep. [Within.] The queen, where is she?

Cleopatra.

2545He comes too late to invade the rights of death.

2547Coward flesh,
2548Wouldst thou conspire with Cæsar to betray me,

Iras.

2554Now, Charmion, to be worthy
2555Of our great queen and mistress.

Cleopatra.

2556Already, death, I feel thee in my veins:

Enter SERAPION, two Priests, ALEXAS bound, Egyptians.

Priest.

Now part us, if thou canst. Behold, Serapion,
2565What havoc death has made!

What havoc death has made! 'Twas what I feared. –
2566Charmion, is this well done?

Charmion.

2567Yes, 'tis well done, and like a queen, the last
2568Of her great race: I follow her.

Alexas.

Of her great race: I follow her. 'Tis true,
2569She has done well: Much better thus to die,

2571See, see how the lovers sit in state together,

2573The impression of a smile, left in her face,

2582No lovers lived so great, or died so well.

EPILOGUE

2583Poets, like disputants, when reasons fail,
2584Have one sure refuge left – and that's to rail.
2585Fop, coxcomb, fool, are thundered through the pit;
2586And this is all their equipage of wit.
2587We wonder how the devil this difference grows,
2588Betwixt our fools in verse, and yours in prose:
2589For, 'faith, the quarrel rightly understood,
2590'Tis civil war with their own flesh and blood.
2591The threadbare author hates the gaudy coat;
2592And swears at the gilt coach, but swears afoot:
2593For 'tis observed of every scribbling man,
2594He grows a fop as fast as e'er he can;
2595Prunes up, and asks his oracle, the glass,
2596If pink or purple best become his face.
2597For our poor wretch, he neither rails nor prays;
2598Nor likes your with just as you like his plays;
2599He has not yet so much of Mr. Bayes.
2600He does his best; and if he cannot please,
2601Would quietly sue out his writ of ease .
2602Yet, if he might his own grand jury call,
2603By the fair sex he begs to stand or fall.
2604Let Cæsar's power the men's ambition move,
2605But grace you him who lost the world for love!
2606Yet if some antiquated lady say,
2607The last age is not copied in his play;
2608Heaven help the man who for that face must drudge,
2609Which only has the wrinkles of a judge.
2610Let not the young and beauteous join with those;
2611For should you raise such numerous hosts of foes,
2612Young wits and sparks he to his aid must call;
2613'Tis more than one man's work to please you all.

  • Dolabela, su amigo
  • Alexas, eunuco de la reina
  • Serapión, sacerdote de la diosa Isis
  • Miris, otro sacerdote
  • Criados de Antonio
  • Cleopatra, reina de Egipto
  • Octavia, esposa de Antonio
